newsitem.title: USA: Clinton sees some "dissent" in Chinese Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: Clinton sees some "dissent" in Chinese Hong Kong.

text.p: As China took control of Hong Kong from Britain on Monday, President Bill Clinton said he expected China would be obliged to allow some "dissent" in the territory under its 1984 agreement with Britain.

Referring to the pact under which China's communist rulers agreed to maintain the lifestyle of the vibrant and freewheeling financial and manufacturing centre, Clinton told reporters: "We expect that they will honour that agreement."

Asked if he believed China would allow "an enclave of dissent" in Hong Kong, he said: "The agreement says that there will be one China and two systems. And it's hard to have a system with free elections and freedom of speech and open press without dissent."
He added: "I can't imagine how you could have it any other way."
Clinton was speaking as he left the White House on a trip to New York and Boston.

Asked about the early entry of hundreds of Chinese troops into Hong Kong even as ceremonies went ahead marking the handover, the president said: "It's a concern, I think. We don't know that they intend to violate the agreement. They may be concerned about disruption, disorder, we'll just have to see what happens. We will monitor it closely."

Of the 1984 agreement, he said: "It's probably the most well-publicised agreement of its kind in modern history and everybody has a pretty good feel for not only the economic but the political system of Hong Kong."

U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, in Hong Kong for the handover, expressed concern about the replacement at midnight of the elected Hong Kong legislature with an assembly named at Beijing's direction and urged quick new elections.
